title: They thought it was over.
paragraphs: The decree had already been sealed. The date was set. The destruction of an entire people—men, women, children—was no longer a threat. It was scheduled.
And the man behind it all slept peacefully.
That’s how evil often feels when it thinks it has won.
The story unfolds in the book of Book of Esther, but don’t read it like distant history. Read it like a mirror. Because what happened to Haman isn’t just about him.
It’s about what God does when wicked plans reach their peak.
Haman didn’t stumble into power—he was consumed by it.
A high official in the Persian Empire, second only to the king, he demanded honor. Not respect—worship. And when one man, Mordecai, refused to bow, something dark ignited inside him.
The kind of rage that doesn’t just want correction—it wants annihilation.
So Haman devised a plan that went far beyond personal revenge. He manipulated King Ahasuerus into signing a decree that would wipe out the entire Jewish people.
And here’s what most people don’t realize…

No thunder.
No interruption.
No visible resistance.
That silence is where most people misread God.
You think because nothing happens immediately… nothing is happening at all.
But behind closed doors, unseen threads were already being pulled.
Esther was placed in the palace long before the crisis.
A Jewish woman crowned queen in a foreign empire? That wasn’t luck.
And when the decree reached her, she faced a choice that exposes something deeper than fear.
“Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14)
She could stay silent and survive temporarily… or speak and risk everything.
You’ve stood in that moment before.
Not just for execution… for spectacle.
But Scripture doesn’t just record events—it reveals patterns.
“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)
He just didn’t know it yet.
The turning point didn’t come with an army.
One night, the king couldn’t sleep. So he ordered the royal chronicles to be read. And there, buried in forgotten records, was the account of Mordecai saving the king’s life.
Haman walks in, ready to request Mordecai’s execution.
Before he can speak, the king asks:
“What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?”
And Haman—blinded by pride—assumes it’s about him.

Royal robes.
A royal horse.
Public honor.
The man he planned to kill.
The man he now had to honor… publicly.
At Esther’s banquet, truth finally surfaced.
“There is a gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman made for Mordecai.”
The very instrument Haman built for another became the instrument of his own judgment.
“Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling.” (Proverbs 26:27)
This is where the story stops being history… and starts confronting you.
Because Haman’s sin wasn’t just hatred.
The belief that he could define justice, manipulate outcomes, and eliminate anything that challenged his authority.

The resentment you justified.
The control you demanded.
The silent contempt you nurtured.
But here’s the difference between Haman and redemption:
He stood exposed… but not transformed.
And exposure without repentance leads to destruction.
Because this is where the Gospel breaks in.
You and I have built gallows too.
Maybe not physical ones—but spiritual ones.
Through sin, rebellion, pride—we’ve constructed the very thing that should condemn us.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
God didn’t just reverse a plan in Esther.
He fulfilled a greater reversal in Jesus Christ.
The cross—the instrument meant for punishment—became the place of salvation.
Jesus took the judgment we built.
He stood where we should have stood.
“So that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)
Now you’re standing where Esther once stood.
You can walk away unchanged—like Haman, exposed but unrepentant.
And receive the grace you did nothing to deserve.
Don’t keep this to yourself either—someone you know is still sleeping under a decree they don’t even realize is hanging over them. Send this to them.
Follow this path if you’re ready to go deeper—not for religion, but for truth that confronts and transforms.
